title: Cable lobby to sue Trump FCC over repeal of national TV ownership cap
gist: Cable lobby groups representing Comcast, Charter and Cox will sue the FCC over its repeal of the 39 percent National Television Ownership cap, arguing Congress set the cap by statute in 2004 and that bigger broadcast groups will extract higher retransmission fees; the FCC argues it can repeal the cap outside the quadrennial review.

insights.claim: Cable groups argue that letting broadcast station groups exceed the national cap gives them leverage to demand higher retransmission fees from TV providers, raising consumer bills.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Broadcast consolidation shifts bargaining power and margin from pay-TV distributors to station groups.
insights.quote: larger broadcast TV station groups will have leverage to demand higher retransmission fees from TV providers

insights.claim: A federal judge, in DirecTV's antitrust suit, found the Nexstar/Tegna deal would raise retransmission consent fees and enjoined the companies from integrating; cable groups call that harm 'merely a preview' of wider consolidation.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The Nexstar/Tegna injunction is a live test of whether consolidation-driven fee increases can be blocked in court.
insights.quote: merely a preview of the further massive broadcast industry consolidation and higher consumer prices
insights.locator: A federal judge ordered Nexstar and Tegna

insights.claim: The Nexstar/Tegna combination would reach 80 percent of US TV households, or 54.5 percent with the UHF discount, and the Carr FCC waived the cap to approve it even before repealing the rule.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Shows the scale of consolidation the repeal enables, well beyond the 39 percent limit.
insights.quote: The Nexstar/Tegna combination would reach 80 percent of TV households in the US, or 54.5 percent

insights.claim: The cable side has itself consolidated: Charter completed its purchase of Cox in August after the FCC rejected protests that it would create unchecked gatekeeper power over Internet distribution.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Both sides of the retrans negotiation are consolidating, making this a scale-vs-scale bargaining fight.

insights.claim: The FCC voted to eliminate the ownership rule on August 6 but only published the order October 1; the author suggests the unusual delay may reflect time spent shoring up legal arguments ahead of lawsuits.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The FCC itself appears to anticipate serious litigation risk.
insights.quote: The delay may be explained by the extra time required for the FCC to shore up its legal arguments
insights.locator: The FCC voted to eliminate the TV ownership rule

insights.claim: Cable groups argue Congress made the 39 percent cap statutory in the 2004 Consolidated Appropriations Act, responding to an FCC attempt to raise it to 45 percent, and explicitly barred forbearance for entities exceeding it.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: If courts accept the statutory reading, the repeal fails and consolidation deals premised on it stall.
insights.quote: Congress established the National Cap at 39 percent in the 2004 CAA [Consolidated Appropriations Act] in direct response to the FCC’s attempt to aggressively raise the Cap to 45 percent

insights.claim: The FCC argues Congress directed it to modify its rules rather than enacting a fixed cap, and that while it cannot change the cap during quadrennial reviews, it can eliminate it outside that process.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The case hinges on a narrow statutory-interpretation question that courts will decide.
insights.quote: directing the Commission to modify its rules rather than by enacting a fixed cap into law.

insights.claim: The cable petition to the FCC is mainly procedural; groups plan to sue in a US appeals court once the order hits the Federal Register and then seek a preliminary injunction to keep the cap in place during litigation.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A preliminary injunction would freeze broadcast M&A dependent on the repeal for the duration of litigation.
